title: The fake Umberto Eco created with AI: a performance that fooled intellectuals
key_facts: A fake page from Umberto Eco's L'Espresso column La Bustina di Minerva, dated 11 April 2010 and titled 'The Machine That Will Have Read Everything', spread on social media as Eco's prophecy about AI
Readers, professors, journalists and Nobel physicist Giorgio Parisi shared it as genuine; Eco never wrote it
Fact-checkers Open, BUTAC, Tlon and Mac Peer exposed it; media scholar and known prankster Ciro Ascione then admitted authorship
Ascione posted the text on Facebook on 1 Oct 2026 and said he produced it in half an hour with ChatGPT
Clues: an image-generator artifact under the opening letter, and 11 April 2010 was a Sunday when L'Espresso was not on sale; the real column that week ran on 16 April 2010
The fake text imagined machines that 'continue a sentence', students gaming AI essays and model collapse
Fellow troll Ermes Maiolica called it 'the new Sistine Chapel of trolling'
quote_evidence: There was, however, one crucial detail: Umberto Eco never wrote that text.
On October 1, 2026, Ascione published the text of the fake "Bustina" on his Facebook page, transcribing it in its entirety and presenting it as authentic.
"Over the past two days," Ascione later wrote, "a fake story I produced in half an hour using ChatGPT has been setting the agenda for the national debate on Artificial Intelligence."
why_it_matters_hint: A half-hour ChatGPT forgery fooled Italy's cultural elite and showed how thin fact-checking habits are
notes: Article is a machine translation of the Italian original; several fact-check outlets and the author's own admission support the facts.
